hook: Drop slices of potato into salty water and in an hour they go limp; leave them in plain water and they turn crisp. Water potential predicts which way water will move, and the formula sheet gives you the equation to put a number on it. The arithmetic is short, but nearly every lost point comes from the same three slips: i, kelvin and the sign.

options: higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) water potential
lower water potential to higher water potential
higher solute concentration to lower solute concentration
prereq.why: Water moves down its water potential gradient, toward the more negative Ψ, which is where solutes are more concentrated.

prereq.q: What does turgor pressure do to a plant cell's pressure potential?
options: Makes it positive, raising the cell's water potential
Makes it negative, lowering the cell's water potential
Has no effect; pressure potential depends on solutes alone
prereq.why: A turgid cell pushes on its wall and the wall pushes back, so ΨP is positive and adds to Ψ.

figure.caption: Ψ = ΨP + Ψs. The open beaker has ΨP = 0; the turgid cell has ΨP > 0. Water moves toward the more negative water potential, here out of the cell.

chain.cause: A solute dissolves and each formula unit makes i particles (1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl).
chain.effect: The concentration of dissolved particles is i × C.

chain.cause: Dissolved particles attract and hold water molecules, lowering water's tendency to move.
chain.effect: Solute potential is negative and proportional to particles and temperature: Ψs = −iCRT.

chain.cause: R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) is defined per kelvin.
chain.effect: T must be in kelvin (°C + 273), and the answer comes out in bars.

chain.cause: A cell wall pushing back on a swollen cell adds pressure; an open beaker adds none.
chain.effect: Water potential is Ψ = ΨP + Ψs, with ΨP = 0 in an open container.

chain.cause: A cell and its surroundings have different water potentials.
chain.effect: Net water moves from the higher (less negative) Ψ to the lower (more negative) Ψ until they are equal.

ideas: Worked example. 0.30 M sucrose, 22 °C, open beaker. i = 1, C = 0.30 mol/L, R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K), T = 295 K. Ψs = −(1)(0.30)(0.0831)(295) = −7.35 bars. ΨP = 0, so Ψ = −7.35 bars (−0.74 MPa).
Same molarity is not same water potential: 0.1 M NaCl (i = 2) has Ψs = −4.95 bars at 25 °C, twice the 0.1 M sucrose value of −2.48 bars.
A potato-core graph crossing 0% mass change at about 0.30 M sucrose means the cells' Ψ equals that solution's Ψ: about −7.4 bars at 22 °C.
Three classic slips: using °C instead of kelvin, forgetting i for salts, and dropping the minus sign.

misconception.wrong: Two solutions with the same molar concentration have the same water potential.
misconception.right: Water potential depends on the number of dissolved particles. 0.1 M NaCl makes about 0.2 M of ions (i = 2), so its Ψ is about twice as negative as 0.1 M sucrose (i = 1).

summary: Water potential is Ψ = ΨP + Ψs. Solute potential is Ψs = −iCRT: i is the number of particles per formula unit (1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl), C the molar concentration, R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) and T the temperature in kelvin. In an open container ΨP = 0. Water moves from higher to lower water potential. 10 bars = 1 MPa.
